Hampi
------------------------------------------
If there is one historical site in India that can make our hearts swell in pride, feel outraged and also depressed—all at the same time—it is हम्पि, the site of Vijayanagara, the great capital of a great empire of that name.
The present हम्पि, a small town in the Bellary district of the Karnataka State, is situated on the south bank of the river Tuṅgabhadrā, at a distance of 360 kms. (225 miles) to the north of the capital city of Bangalore and 77 kms. (48 miles) from the Bellary town.
According to the local legends this place was originally known as पम्पा, a name of the goddess पार्वती. She performed तपस् (austerities) here to get शिव as her husband and ultimately succeeded in marrying him here! That is why the Lord शिव of this place (Virūpākṣa) is also known as Pampāpati (husband of पम्पा or पार्वती).
Historically, this city was built by the princes हरिहर and Bukka in A.
under the inspiration of the great sage विद्यारण्य (A.

-1386).
The kingdom that developed around it was ruled by the kings of four dynasties: Saṅgama; Sāḷuva; Tuḷuva; and, Āravaṭi.
हम्पि विरूपाक्ष तेम्प्ले">A view of हम्पि Virūpākṣa TempleThe greatest of them was Kṛṣṇadevarāya (A.
-1529), during whose reign it attained maximum prosperity and fame. Many foreign travellers like Nicolode Comte (15th century A. D.), Abdul Razak (A.

) have left glorious accounts of the empire.
Today, it is an important tourist spot with several sites and ruins of historical and archaeological significance. Many of these are connected—as per the local legends, but based on the Rāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki—with राम, सीता, सुग्रीव, हनुमान् and वालि of yore.
The following is a selected list of the more important places of sight-seeing. For the sake of convenience they have been arranged in the alphabetical order.
Elephant Stables
This has ten domed chambers. It is in the north of the complex. Elephants used to be kept in chains here.
Gaṇeśa Images
They are situated on the south-eastern slope of the हेमकूट hill. The smaller one is 2.5 metres (8 ft.) high and the larger one 4.5 metres (15 ft.).
Hajāra राम Temple
This is believed to have been the private temple of the royal family. It has several relief figures on its walls, depicting the scenes from the Rāmāyaṇa, mostly those related to the events in the town of किष्किन्धा, capital of वालि/Sugrīva.
Hampi Bazaar
This was the main business centre of the Vijayanagara city. It starts from the विरूपाक्ष तेम्प्ले. It is 10 metres (33 ft.) wide and 730 metres (2400 ft.) long. On either side there are ruins of the old buildings.
Hemakūṭa Hill
This is a small hill overlooking the हम्पि Bazaar. It contains a group of pre-Vijayanagara temples belonging to the period 9th to the 11th century A. D.
King’s Balance
Situated near the famous Viṭṭhala temple is the king’s Balance. It is a granite arch 4.5 metres (15 ft.) in height and 3.6 metres (12 ft.) in width. It was being used to hang a balance to weigh the king against valuables to be gifted away on special days. (This is generally called ‘tulāpuruṣadāna’.)
Kodaṇḍarāma Temple
Situated at the spot where राम is said to have crowned सुग्रीव as the king of किष्किन्धा (before killing वालि) this temple contains large images of राम (with his bow Kodaṇḍa) and लक्ष्मण.
Lotus Mahal
This seems to be a part of the zenana or women’s quarters. The ground floor is an open pavilion. The upper floor has windows and balcony. There is also a moat around the building.
Mahānavamī Dibba
This is a massive stone basement, of what, perhaps, remains of a pillared hall of many storeys where the great festival of Navarātri used to be celebrated gorgeously.
Narasiṁha Image
This is a monolith image of नरसिṁह (Man-lion, the fourth इन्चर्नतिओन् of Lord विष्णु), near the हेमकूट hill. It is 7 metres (22 ft.) in height. It is badly mutilated.
Virūpākṣa Temple
This is the main temple of the whole campus. Its deity was the god of the royal family. (See VIRŪPĀKṢA TEMPLE for details.)
Viṭṭhala Temple
Situated on the southern bank of the Tuṅgabhadrā river, it is the most ornate of all the temples in the campus. It is dedicated to Viṭṭhala, an aspect of कृष्ण. Its special features are: musical pillars of stone, sculptures of Varāha and other incarnations of विष्णु, pillars with carved forms of नरसिṁह and the stone रथ or chariot. This temple was never completed. It is a World Heritage Monument, one of the three in South India.
There is a nice Archaeological Museum in the nearby Kāmalāpuram village.
